# Obama accepts historic Democratic nomination before massive Denver crowd

**DENVER, Colorado (CNN)** — Barack Obama accepted the Democratic presidential nomination Thursday night before more than 75,000 people at Denver’s Invesco Field, becoming the first African American to lead a major U.S. political party’s presidential ticket.

Standing on a large outdoor stage on the final night of the Democratic National Convention, the Illinois senator framed the 2008 election as a choice between change and what he described as the failed policies of the past eight years.

“With profound gratitude and great humility, I accept your nomination for the presidency of the United States,” Obama told the cheering crowd.

The address came 45 years to the day after the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech in Washington. Obama did not dwell on the historic nature of his nomination, focusing instead on the economy, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, health care and energy policy.

He sharply criticized Republican nominee John McCain, arguing that the Arizona senator would continue many of President George W. Bush’s policies.

“John McCain has voted with George Bush 90 percent of the time,” Obama said. “I don’t know about you, but I’m not ready to take a 10 percent chance on change.”

Obama also sought to answer Republican claims that he lacked the experience and resolve to serve as commander in chief. He pledged to end the war in Iraq responsibly, strengthen efforts against al Qaeda and pursue diplomacy while maintaining a strong military.

On domestic policy, Obama promised tax relief for working families, broader access to health insurance and investment in alternative energy. He tied those proposals to what he called “the American promise” — the idea that people who work hard should have a fair chance to succeed.

The stadium setting marked a departure from the traditional convention finale inside an arena. Campaign officials said the move allowed tens of thousands of additional supporters to attend, underscoring the grassroots enthusiasm that powered Obama through a long primary battle with Sen. Hillary Clinton.

Clinton and her husband, former President Bill Clinton, had used their convention speeches to urge party unity and endorse Obama. His running mate, Delaware Sen. Joe Biden, accepted the vice presidential nomination a night earlier.

Obama closed the convention by calling on voters to reject cynicism and take part in the election.

“America, we cannot turn back,” he said. “Not with so much work to be done.”

The speech formally launched the general-election phase of Obama’s campaign against McCain, who was set to accept the Republican nomination the following week.

**DENVER, Aug. 28, 2008** — Barack Obama accepted the Democratic presidential nomination Thursday night before more than 80,000 people at Invesco Field, where attendees described an atmosphere that shifted from festival-like anticipation to near silence as the Illinois senator delivered one of the most closely watched speeches of the campaign.

Inside the stadium, delegates and members of the public waved American flags and held blue “Change” signs beneath towering video screens. Long security lines and hours of waiting preceded the prime-time program, but the crowd repeatedly erupted as Obama criticized Republican nominee John McCain, discussed the economy and wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and invoked the 45th anniversary of Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech.

Obama promised “change you can believe in” while arguing that the election was not simply about him, but about Americans struggling with wages, health care, education and rising costs. His appearance on a stage framed by columns drew cheers and also prompted Republican criticism that the setting was overly theatrical.

The loudest moment came at the close, when Obama’s family joined him and fireworks burst above the stadium. Attendees remained in the stands taking photographs on compact cameras and mobile phones as confetti fell and music played.

Citizen journalists documented the night in real time through blogs, text updates, photographs and early social-media posts. From seats throughout the stadium, they recorded chants, crowd reactions and the difficulties of moving through packed concourses. Some reported overloaded cellular networks as thousands of people attempted to call, text or upload images simultaneously.

Outside Invesco Field, the experience was more fragmented. Ticket holders passed through extensive security checkpoints while police controlled nearby streets and restricted access around the venue. Vendors, volunteers and demonstrators gathered beyond the secured perimeter, and citizen reporters moved among them with handheld cameras and laptops, offering perspectives largely absent from the television networks’ tightly produced coverage.

Protest activity in Denver had led to arrests and confrontations earlier in the convention week, although the immediate area around the stadium was heavily secured Thursday. Those without credentials watched from designated areas, bars and public gatherings, while independent reporters posted accounts of police lines, road closures and the contrast between the celebration inside and the tense security presence outside.

The event marked the first time a major-party presidential nominee accepted the nomination before a stadium-sized audience. For those inside, the night ended as a choreographed political spectacle. For those reporting from the sidewalks and security barriers, it was also a story of crowds, restricted movement and a new generation using mobile technology to chronicle a national political moment firsthand.

## Obama Makes History Before a Diverse American Crowd

**DENVER, Aug. 28, 2008** — Barack Obama became the first African American to accept the Democratic Party’s presidential nomination Thursday, addressing a vast and visibly diverse crowd on the 45th anniversary of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech.

More than 80,000 people filled Denver’s open-air Invesco Field for the final night of the Democratic National Convention. The audience—Black, white, Latino, Asian American, Native American, young and old—reflected the broad coalition that had carried the Illinois senator through a closely contested primary campaign and to a milestone unprecedented in the history of a major American political party.

With his wife, Michelle, and their daughters watching, Obama formally accepted the nomination and presented his candidacy as both a historic achievement and a call for national unity.

“With profound gratitude and great humility, I accept your nomination for the presidency of the United States,” he told the cheering crowd.

The date gave the occasion added resonance. Exactly 45 years earlier, on Aug. 28, 1963, King had stood before the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington and described his dream of a nation in which people would be judged by their character rather than the color of their skin.

Obama did not make King’s anniversary the central theme of his address. Instead, he focused on the economy, health care, energy policy, national security and his differences with Republican nominee John McCain. Yet the historical connection was unmistakable: An African American was accepting a major party’s nomination before a stadium audience that embodied, in many ways, the more inclusive America envisioned by the civil rights movement.

The setting reinforced that symbolism. Delegates shared the stands with tens of thousands of ordinary voters, creating a crowd far larger and more varied than the audience typically assembled inside a convention hall. Families, students, veterans, union members and longtime civil rights activists watched together as Obama stepped onto the stage.

For many in attendance, the moment linked generations. Some remembered the segregation and racial violence that King confronted; others had grown up after the passage of landmark civil rights laws. Together, they witnessed a political breakthrough made possible by decades of activism, sacrifice and expanding participation in American democracy.

Obama acknowledged that the country still faced deep divisions and serious challenges. His nomination, while historic, did not erase racial inequality or fulfill King’s dream. But the scene in Denver marked a powerful measure of change: 45 years after King spoke of an unfinished promise, a diverse American crowd gathered to see a Black candidate stand at the center of a presidential campaign.

The night was therefore both political and symbolic—a party convention culminating in a nomination, and a national milestone unfolding on an anniversary charged with memory. As applause swept through the stadium, the distance between the March on Washington and the Denver convention seemed at once immense and remarkably close.

## Obama accepts Democratic nomination before a packed Denver stadium

**DENVER, Colorado —** Barack Obama closed the 2008 Democratic National Convention on Thursday night by accepting his party’s presidential nomination before more than 80,000 people at Invesco Field, transforming the convention’s final session into a mixture of political rally, outdoor concert and historic celebration.

The Illinois senator became the first African American to accept the presidential nomination of a major U.S. political party. The moment came 45 years to the day after the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech in Washington.

“With profound gratitude and great humility, I accept your nomination for the presidency of the United States,” Obama told the crowd.

Supporters answered with chants of **“Obama! Obama!”** and **“Yes we can!”** American flags filled the stadium, and delegates waved blue placards as fireworks erupted after the speech. Obama was joined onstage by his wife, Michelle, their daughters, Malia and Sasha, and vice presidential nominee Joe Biden and his family.

### From convention hall to football stadium

The decision to move the final night from Denver’s Pepsi Center to the home of the Denver Broncos allowed tens of thousands of members of the public to attend. The larger venue also produced a scene uncommon for a political convention: long security lines, packed concourses, music between speeches and spectators performing the wave while waiting for the main program.

CNN iReport contributors in and around the stadium described the atmosphere with phrases such as **“electric”** and **“like a rock concert.”** Others emphasized the diversity of the audience—longtime Democratic activists, first-time conventiongoers, families and young volunteers who had traveled to Denver specifically for Obama’s acceptance speech.

Among the more conspicuous supporters were people wearing **“Rednecks for Obama”** shirts and buttons. Their presence drew attention because it played against assumptions about Obama’s appeal in rural and working-class white communities. The slogan was partly humorous, but those displaying it said their support was serious and centered on economic concerns, the Iraq war and dissatisfaction with the Bush administration.

### A difficult trip to the stadium

Getting to and from Invesco Field was less festive. Streets around the stadium were closed or tightly controlled, and delegates were transported on designated buses. Light-rail cars and downtown transit stations were crowded for hours, while many attendees walked long distances from central Denver.

Security screening created substantial lines before the program. After Obama’s speech, the simultaneous departure of tens of thousands of people produced another crush around pedestrian routes, shuttle areas and rail platforms. Some attendees waited through several trains or buses before finding space. Despite the congestion, the evening proceeded without a major security incident.

### Dean opens the final session

Democratic National Committee Chairman **Howard Dean**, whose 50-state strategy had pushed the party to compete beyond its traditional strongholds, helped launch the evening’s political program. Dean argued that Democrats could win in every part of the country and presented the convention as evidence of a broader, more nationally competitive party.

The former Vermont governor praised organizers and volunteers and urged Democrats to carry the stadium’s enthusiasm into registration drives, canvassing and Election Day turnout.

### Richardson attacks McCain

New Mexico Gov. **Bill Richardson**, who had challenged Obama during the Democratic primaries before endorsing him, delivered one of the night’s sharper attacks on Republican nominee John McCain.

Richardson contrasted McCain’s image as an independent-minded “maverick” with his support for many Bush administration policies. He also used one of the convention’s better-known jokes: McCain might spend heavily on shoes, Richardson said, but Americans would pay for his **“flip-flops.”**

Richardson, one of the country’s most prominent Hispanic elected officials, also addressed portions of his remarks in Spanish. His appearance underscored the importance of Latino voters in New Mexico, Colorado, Nevada and other states that Obama’s campaign hoped to move into the Democratic column.

### Gore frames the election as a national turning point

Former Vice President **Al Gore** received a prolonged ovation when he took the stage. Eight years after the disputed 2000 election, Gore used his speech to connect Obama’s candidacy to the issues that had defined his own post-political career, particularly climate change and energy independence.

Gore argued that the country faced intertwined economic, national-security and environmental crises. He compared the political obstacles confronting Obama with those faced by Abraham Lincoln, another Illinois politician who entered the White House at a time of national division.

“The choice is clear,” Gore said, portraying Obama as the candidate of change and McCain as an extension of President George W. Bush’s policies.

Gore’s presence also served as a reminder of the Democrats’ narrow loss in 2000. His message was not simply that supporters should be inspired, but that they should vote and organize so the election would not be decided by a small number of ballots.

### Celebrities mix with delegates and volunteers

The stadium crowd included a conspicuous entertainment contingent. **Oprah Winfrey**, one of Obama’s earliest and most influential celebrity supporters, watched from the audience. Filmmaker **Spike Lee** was also among the recognizable faces in Denver.

The evening’s musical program included performances by **Stevie Wonder**, **Sheryl Crow**, **John Legend** and **will.i.am**, while **Jennifer Hudson** sang the national anthem. The celebrity presence added to the concertlike atmosphere, although the program remained focused on veterans, working families and ordinary voters whose stories reinforced the campaign’s economic message.

### Obama turns from biography to confrontation

Obama’s speech was more combative than many of his earlier national addresses. After recounting his family history and praising Hillary Clinton, Biden and other Democratic leaders, he directly challenged McCain on the economy, taxes, health care, education and foreign policy.

He tied McCain to Bush and used a line that became one of the speech’s central themes: **“Eight is enough.”** The crowd quickly adopted the phrase as another chant.

Obama also answered Republican criticism that his message of change was too abstract. He promised tax relief for most working families, an end to tax breaks for companies that moved jobs overseas, expanded access to health insurance and a long-term effort to reduce dependence on foreign oil.

On foreign policy, he pledged to end the war in Iraq responsibly, focus on al Qaeda and rebuild alliances. He praised McCain’s military service but argued that honorable service did not make McCain’s policy judgments correct.

The address also sought to balance partisan criticism with a call for a less destructive political culture. Obama said Democrats and Republicans could disagree about abortion, guns, immigration and same-sex relationships without questioning one another’s patriotism or character.

### A carefully staged historic ending

The setting was designed for television as well as for the audience in Denver. Obama spoke from a large columned stage, with the stadium crowd forming a sweeping backdrop. Critics compared the architecture to a classical temple, while the campaign said the design was intended to evoke familiar American civic buildings.

As Obama concluded, supporters again shouted **“Yes we can.”** Biden and both candidates’ families joined him while confetti fell and fireworks lit the sky above the stadium.

For many attendees, the historic character of the nomination outweighed the spectacle. iReporters described strangers embracing, crying and taking photographs of the stage long after the formal program ended. Even as the crowd confronted packed trains, slow-moving buses and long walks back toward downtown Denver, the chants continued outside the stadium.

The convention had begun with lingering divisions from the long Obama-Clinton primary fight. It ended with Democrats presenting a unified ticket, a stadium full of supporters and Obama asking voters to make the election a verdict on eight years of Republican leadership.

“This moment,” he said near the close of his address, was the time to keep faith with the American promise—and to begin the work of changing the country.
